title: Second Bisleri Sample Found Unsafe as FSSAI Sanctions Prosecution Over Bacteria
excerpt: A batch from Bisleri's West Bengal plant tested positive for coliform bacteria in two laboratories, the regulator has barred its sale and sanctioned prosecution, and the company says its own independent tests found the same batch safe.
body:
• India's food regulator FSSAI has found a second Bisleri sample unsafe: a batch from the company's West Bengal plant tested positive for coliform bacteria in both primary and referral laboratory tests, according to Reuters.
  • The affected batch, PB 201, was made at Bisleri's Telipara plant in Jalpaiguri district; its sale was prohibited on August 12 and FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against the company.
  • Bisleri says it recalled the batch in August and that independent testing at FSSAI-recognised laboratories found the same batch met all applicable standards; it has asked the regulator to review the sampling and testing process.
  • Reader check: the prohibition covers batch PB 201 only, not all Bisleri production. If you have a bottle from that batch, do not drink it and follow the recall.

Indian authorities have found a sample of Bisleri-branded water unsafe due to coliform bacteria, the second such finding to come to light in recent days against India's biggest packaged-water brand, Reuters reported on Saturday, citing a regulatory document it had seen.

In a notice dated August 12, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) told Bisleri the sample was "non-conforming (UNSAFE)" and that it showed the presence of coliform, and asked the company to prohibit the sale of the affected batch, which was manufactured in July. A government official told Reuters the sample was tested again for confirmation and was still found unsafe.

One batch, one plant

The sample was taken from Bisleri's facility at Telipara in Jalpaiguri district, West Bengal, The Hindu BusinessLine reported. Both the primary and referral laboratories confirmed the presence of coliform bacteria, which led to the sale prohibition on batch PB 201 and to FSSAI sanctioning prosecution against Bisleri International. It is the second prosecution sanction against the company in recent days: a sample collected from one of its plants in Goa also failed testing, BusinessLine reported.

The bacteria finding follows a separate first finding this week in which the regulator said a Bisleri sample was unsafe because of chemicals that health agencies say may cause cancer. Court records in that case show the regulator has initiated prosecution proceedings, which could include a jail term and a fine for manufacturing a sample found unsafe, according to Reuters.

Bisleri disputes the result

Mumbai-based Bisleri told Reuters it had recalled the batch in August on the government's instructions. "The primary and referral laboratories reported the presence of coliform bacteria in the regulatory sample," the company said. But Bisleri said independent testing it commissioned, at FSSAI-recognised laboratories, found samples from the same batch met the applicable standard for coliform bacteria and all other applicable food safety standards.

"The difference between the regulatory and independent findings warrants a thorough review. Bisleri will continue to cooperate fully with FSSAI to establish the facts."

— Bisleri International, statement to Reuters

The company has asked FSSAI to examine the sampling process, testing methodology and laboratory findings, and any factors that may have contributed to the variation in results. The regulator did not immediately respond to a request for comment, Reuters reported.

A wider crackdown on bottled water

The findings land on a brand that is a household staple in India. Bisleri's 20-cent bottles have made it the market leader in India's $3.5 billion packaged drinking-water market, competing with PepsiCo and Coca-Cola; the company says it has 130 operational plants and 5,980 distributors. Poor water quality has made bottled water a necessity for many homes and restaurants.

FSSAI has used the findings to widen oversight of the whole sector. The regulator has directed state food safety commissioners and regional directors to have food safety officers conduct regular inspections and risk-based sampling of packaged drinking water and mineral water, warning that appropriate action will be initiated in cases of non-compliance. Official sources told BusinessLine that samples of other brands have also been lifted and their facilities inspected, so Bisleri is unlikely to be the last name in this round of enforcement.

What to check

The sale prohibition is specific: it covers batch PB 201 from the West Bengal plant, not every Bisleri bottle on sale. Readers who buy packaged water in India can check the batch number printed on the bottle; anyone holding a bottle from batch PB 201 should not consume it. The larger question the dispute now turns on is methodological: two sets of laboratories, testing samples from the same batch, have reached opposite conclusions, and FSSAI's review of that gap will decide whether this remains a single-batch recall or becomes a broader judgment on how India's bottled-water testing is done.
